The overwhelming support from the world of football for Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray has come as no surprise to interim head coach Damien Johnson.

Mowbray announced on Wednesday he was stepping back from his role at the Championship club because of health challenges with Johnson and Mike Dodds taking charge "for the time being".

The news sparked an outpouring of messages of support from EFL clubs and further afield.

"To someone like me, it's not a surprise," Johnson said.

"I've known him for over 10 years, but I think people who have only known him in this club for the four or five months he's been in, they can see that. That's just the impact Tony has on people, it's just a testament to Tony and his nature and how he is and how he treats people.".

Mowbray, 62, returned to Ewood Park in June for a second spell as head coach and has taken them to 13th place in the Championship after they finished just five points clear of the relegation zone last season.

The former Middlesbrough and West Brom boss had previously taken time out of the game during his spell as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

Boro head coach Kim Hellberg was one of the first to send his best wishes to one of his predecessors.

It has been revealed that "He's a brilliant guy. It was really good to meet him and he was absolutely brilliant every time I've talked to him," Hellberg said.

Industry observers note that "He's a brilliant football coach. He's done a lot of good things. He's a brilliant human being and you can see everyone knows that.".

Rovers have won five of their past nine league games with Johnson crediting Mowbray's impact at the club for creating a more positive atmosphere.

"When the statement came out there was concern - we care a lot about Tony and it was a little bit of a shock - we want what's best for him at this time," Johnson told BBC Radio Lancashire.

"Tony has built a real bond with the whole group and with everyone at the whole club, so there was naturally concern for him and a bit of emotion for a day or so but we all hold him in the highest regard - we hope he's given the privacy he needs.

Recent findings suggest that "He sent a private message to the players which was read out today [Friday] and they appreciated it. He's sent some private messages to staff but Tony's allowed us just to get on, he'll be allowed the time he needs and we'll just get on with the game.".

Blackburn visit Burnley on Sunday (12:00 GMT) hoping to end a 10-game winless run against their Lancashire rivals, who have not won a home game in the league since 18 October last year.

Johnson indicates the match is their main focus rather than what may happen with the managerial situation down the line.

"We've just been focused fully on the game, we know it's a huge game and we've been working with the team throughout the week. The discussions have been about the game and nothing else," he added.

Meanwhile, Blackburn are set to be without goalkeeper Balazs Toth until the latest year after he told Hungarian media, external he suffered a hand injury while playing for his national side against Northern Ireland on Tuesday.

"The situation is not that good, but for now it looks like I will be able to avoid surgery," he noted before travelling back to England to have the injury assessed by Blackburn.

Streaming services and social platforms are giving internet creators more places to make their next hit show. Disney+ is adding videos from TikTok creators, Netflix is expanding its lineup of creator-led podcasts, and Instagram is testing videos up to 90 minutes long.

In a recent development, but when it comes to what Americans watch on TV, YouTube is still king. In August, it accounted for a record 15.8 percent of U.S. TV watch time, more than twice Netflix’s 7.7 percent and the biggest share of any firm in the rankings.

It has been revealed that this week, YouTube gave us a look at what some of its biggest creators are making, from highlights that are already live to those coming in the months ahead. Here's what’s on the slate.

In a recent development, emma Chamberlain — What Are You Waiting For? Emma Chamberlain hates waiting in line, which makes her an especially good person to ask Upcoming Yorkers why they do it. The 2026 Mashable 101 honoree visits some of the city's busiest lines and talks to the people in them about what’s worth giving up part of their day for. The line is just the starting point for a closer look at the fandoms and subcultures that bring people together in person. The series, produced by Amplify Pictures, premieres on Chamberlain's channel in early 2027.

Grace Reiter — Twilight (but better). After sending up Panem, Mashable 101 creator Grace Reiter is headed to Forks. The Saturday Night Live cast member and 2026 Mashable 101 honoree is directing and improvising her way through a Twilight parody, her second unscripted feature after The Hunger Games (but better), which drew more than 18 million views. The upcoming one premieres Feb. 18 on Reiter's channel.

Aryna Sabalenka — Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered. What does wedding planning look like when most of the year is spent living out of a suitcase? Sabalenka's latest docuseries follows the tennis champion from the tennis tour to dress fittings and brand meetings, including a project to design her own $250,000 diamond necklace. The show expands on her existing YouTube series, Aryna’s Arena, and premieres on her channel in spring 2027.

Wesley Wang — Response, Extract 14, and Absolute Cinema. If your group chat is always trying to solve the murder before the massive reveal, Extract 14 will give you all something to work with. The six-episode mystery hides clues in found footage and offers $100,000 to the first viewer who cracks the case. Wang also has Response, a sci-fi horror short about park rangers who find something unsettling during a welfare check, and Absolute Cinema, which brings 10 aspiring filmmakers to Newly introduced York for a weeklong boot camp. Viewers get the final say on who wins $100,000 to make their movie. Response is due in early 2027, with the other two projects following in the spring.

Nick DiGiovanni — Chef. Nick DiGiovanni went from MasterChef finalist to YouTube food star, building an audience with step-by-step recipes and stunts like making the world’s largest sushi roll. #24811. Latest Update: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Latest Update: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

Recent findings suggest that "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

According to recent reports, for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Industry observers note that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The newly introduced findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Sources indicate that an important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

Sources indicate that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Industry observers note that producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

Sources indicate that to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The latest approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

In a recent development, another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

Recent findings suggest that "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler mentioned. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

In a recent development, the findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

According to recent reports, A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

Industry observers note that the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

It has been revealed that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Sources indicate that rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Breaking: Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.
  • More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.
  • In a recent development, in 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In a recent development, in 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to problem bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, noted Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

In a recent development, countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

According to recent reports, finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

It has been revealed that that means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner mentioned.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner stated.

Sources indicate that germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

In a recent development, philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million revealed this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

In a recent development, "Promises like that always come at the last minute," he remarked. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion.".

This article was originally written in German.

  • Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived.
  • “It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.

Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.

“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.

Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the tech giant, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

Sources indicate that in January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake with a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.

Industry observers note that inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.

Sources indicate that according to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.

Recent findings suggest that “We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”.

One ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.

ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”.

“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek said in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.

Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions—a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.

The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof Latest and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic concerns within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.

“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”.

In a recent development, like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post and accept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses said affects their ability to get shifts; and it offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, and dynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the company’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.

According to recent reports, but when a concern is raised, Vitek remarked, a human reviews it. He said they evaluate claims of “medical malpractice or abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a patient as soon as ShiftKey receives it” and decide if deactivating the worker is “appropriate.” He declined to comment on these specific events, citing reasons of privacy and ongoing litigation. He added there may be instances where ShiftKey is not promptly notified, which can delay action.

After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.

In court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree stated it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lewis’ family.

Industry observers note that A representative for Peachtree Centre declined to comment citing pending litigation. In court, the home pointed out Lewis was admitted to the hospital with many conditions besides effects from the injection, and her death certificate lists “senile degeneration of the brain” as the cause.

As part of the case, Kaye testified that she drove more than 250 miles from Myrtle Beach to work the Peachtree overnight shift. She had over two years of experience at the time and said she wasn’t given so much as a tour before being the only nurse posted to oversee a floor of 22 patients.

Recent findings suggest that “This particular shift I had a lot of patients,” she testified in the August deposition. “It was very overwhelming.”.

In their complaint against Peachtree and ShiftKey, Lewis’ family said they’d entrusted their “vulnerable” mother to a home they expected to “properly train staff.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ll never get Mom back,” noted Lewis’ son, James Lewis, in a deposition earlier this year. “I just don't want it to happen to anybody else.”.

According to recent reports, kara Smith can’t tell you where she’ll be working next week. A certified nursing assistant, Smith logs into the ShiftKey app most mornings to browse eight-hour shifts at more than a dozen long-term care facilities within driving distance from her West Virginia home.

According to recent reports, lured by the promise of scheduling freedom and premium pay for hard-to-fill shifts, Smith became a ShiftKey contractor in 2022. She claims she soon learned it's not unheard of to work night shifts at nursing homes staffed entirely by ShiftKey.

Founded in 2016 in Texas, ShiftKey grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as unprepared nursing homes reeled from rolling outbreaks that could claim dozens of lives in a single facility. Health care workers sought higher pay as their risks mounted, and homes scrambled to fill shifts.

Industry observers note that backed by private equity, ShiftKey and its competitors Clipboard Health and IntelyCare benefited. According to an analysis by the US Department of Health and Human Services, from 2019 to 2022, the use of contract staff in nursing homes tripled from 4 to 12 percent of all nursing hours. Though it’s since declined, the rate remains higher than prepandemic.

In 2023, ShiftKey’s then CEO told Axios that the firm was valued at more than $2 billion.

According to recent reports, nursing homes pay ShiftKey set rates for workers. The platform then “mathematically” calculates a “suggested” rate for each shift posted, Vitek said in a statement, emphasizing that dynamic pricing tools are only used to increase pay for “difficult-to-fill” shifts—and never to decrease rates.

In a recent development, workers then bid to claim it. This bidding system is what got Smith hooked: Instead of accepting whatever wage a facility would offer, Smith haggled for higher pay.

Recent findings suggest that “If I can even make 25 extra cents, I'm going to try to push for that,” noted Smith, a 47-year-old single mom. “Every penny counts.”.

According to recent reports, since the pandemic, however, wages on ShiftKey have plummeted, according to several nurses who spoke with Proof News and WIRED. Teresa, an LPN who declined to give her last name, joined ShiftKey in 2019. She stopped using the platform last year when she noticed competition for shifts growing—and pay rates declining.

“People were fighting over trash shifts for under $20 an hour,” said Teresa, a single mother of three kids.

Smith remembers being able to bid $3 to $4 more an hour above the facility’s suggested rate when she first joined, but this year she mentioned she’s been forced to accept less money or risk no work at all.

According to her ShiftKey payment records that she shared with Proof News and Wired, one facility paid her $32.50 an hour in the summer of 2025 and around $26 a year later. Payments from another nursing home revealed the same downward trend. On Facebook groups, many ShiftKey workers have posted about a similar dip in earnings.

According to recent reports, “The starting bids are shamefully low,” stated Smith. “It’s not worth the workload or the drive.”.

During her four years with ShiftKey, Smith remarked she routinely felt “thrown in” at upcoming facilities without orientation, clear instructions, or logins. She said she had to work hard to familiarize herself with the residents’ conditions, because critical details, such as who is a fall risk or who has a catheter or an ostomy, are frequently missing. Hours in, she felt like she was in “an ocean and nobody’s around me.”.

“We're coming there because they're short-handed,” noted Smith. “So we are automatically going to be walking into a shit show.”.

Sources indicate that smith said a lack of orientation led to scary close calls. Last year, she notes she arrived at a Virginia nursing home with no advance information, not even the door code. She didn’t know anything about the patients, and that made her “very stressed out.”.

“I know my blood pressure went up because of it,” she mentioned.

Another time, Smith said she dropped off a regular drink to a resident only to later learn that they were prescribed only thickened liquids to avoid choking.

“What if they choked and died?” said Smith.

Recent findings suggest that facilities on ShiftKey have the option to require that workers attend a paid “orientation shift” before picking up a regular one. But four ShiftKey workers told Proof News and WIRED that they've frequently picked up nursing home shifts without doing an orientation shift first.

Inspection reports from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services dating back to 2023 and obtained by Proof News and WIRED reveal ShiftKey workers making dangerous mistakes.

In Ohio, after a ShiftKey nurse made a PICC line mistake at Stellar Care Center, a federal inspection report noted that the nursing home’s administrators had never checked to see whether she was trained to do IV therapy.

The report noted that an administrator had spoken with someone at ShiftKey, who told her that because they consider everyone on the app an independent contractor, the manufacturer didn’t test for what skills they knew.

In other cases, the orientation was inadequate. At Woodway Rehabilitation and Healthcare Center in Texas, a federal health surveyor spotted a ShiftKey worker trying to force-feed a resident a health shake using an oral syringe. The ShiftKey worker remarked it was her first time at the facility, according to the 2025 inspection report. She received some orientation for the facility on the app before she started her shift, the report said, but couldn’t remember if feeding was included.

Industry observers note that in 2024, another CMS surveyor wrote that a ShiftKey nurse at the Medical Suites at Oak Creek in Wisconsin told the surveyor she was not shown any care looks for residents on her first day. According to the report, the surveyor spoke with an administrator, who handed the surveyor an undated orientation checklist. The administrator mentioned they did not right now have a policy regarding orientation for gig nurses, but that she'd be implementing one in 30 minutes.

Neither Stellar Care, Woodway Rehab, nor the Medical Suites at Oak Creek responded to requests for comment on this story.

Researchers warn that gig nurses who aren’t properly oriented and who move constantly between facilities can disrupt the continuity of care. Jasmine Travers Altizer, an assistant professor at Newly introduced York University’s Rory Meyers College of Nursing, conducted a qualitative study of 22 nursing home administrators this year and found that they felt relying on temporary workers led to “less consistent care, more hospital transfers, potentially unnecessary treatments and antibiotic use, and increased falls.” Administrators also reported staff having less ability to support one another across the facility.

Gig nursing “shouldn't be a fix for chronic understaffing,” stated Travers Altizer in an email. It's critical, she said, to “have consistent staff who know the residents.”.

In response, Vitek, the ShiftKey CEO, said, “Continuity of care is an key consideration in nursing home quality, but the concern predates platforms like ours.”.

Sources indicate that shiftKey says its model keeps more nurses on the job during a time of critical shortage. Vitek noted a survey of workers on ShiftKey found that more than a third stated they would not be able to stay in the health care industry without such a platform.

“We reject the premise that enabling independent flexible nursing support is harmful to the industry, because the challenge in addressing these concerns is not about the choice between full-time staff versus temporary shift support,” he said.

Sources indicate that katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, stated a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”.

Sources indicate that according to CMS data, the average time worked by nursing staff per resident at Peachtree, where Lewis was accidentally injected, is lower than the state average and less than minimum requirements set by the US Department of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration that are no longer in effect. The American Health Care Association, a nonprofit group that represents nursing homes, successfully challenged the rule in court in 2025, and the Trump administration ultimately withdrew the rule, stating that the move would save nursing homes $55.1 billion over the course of 10 years.

Industry observers note that “We need to have minimum safe staffing levels,” said Hannah Garden-Monheit, who worked on nursing home reform at the White House National Economic Council and now is executive director of Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy. “The patients need that continuity of care.”.

Half a dozen ShiftKey nurses and the two former corporate employees told Proof News and WIRED that many of the facilities that use ShiftKey have a history of poor quality of care and staffing issues.

One ShiftKey nurse recalled rats scurrying in the ceiling and roaches falling from lights at one nursing home.

Constance Hicks, a longtime certified nursing assistant in Connecticut, said that most nursing homes she worked at through ShiftKey were in terrible condition: no barrier cream, no soap, no supplies. Some places had no hot water. Not once in more than a year of picking up shifts through ShiftKey does she remember receiving any training at the homes.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2023, while working a double shift at Cobalt Lodge Healthcare, Hicks discovered an elderly patient with their head and neck trapped in a bed rail, their forehead compressed against the metal, according to court records. She checked the patient’s vitals and, finding dangerously high blood pressure, called 911. Even though her shift had ended, Hicks stayed until emergency workers arrived.

Hicks said she documented everything and sent it to ShiftKey. She also tried reaching out to the company’s representatives but said no one responded. By the next day, her ShiftKey account was deactivated.

Hicks, who indicates the incident with the patient caused “a whole lot of psychological trauma,” tried to file a lawsuit against ShiftKey over the deactivation and other challenges, but court records show the company successfully moved her case to private arbitration.

Cobalt Lodge Healthcare did not respond to a request for comment, and ShiftKey declined, citing ongoing litigation.

Regarding the quality of the facilities, Vitek remarked, “When professionals raise a concern, we encourage them to use the formal reporting channels, and remind them that they can choose whether they can accept future shifts there.”.

Some lawmakers have begun scrutinizing platforms like ShiftKey, in part over concerns that it’s misclassifying its workers as independent contractors.

A gig nurse logs into ShiftKey.

“It's not like they're coming in, bringing their own tools, fixing a pipe, and leaving,” says Emma Greenman, a Minnesota state representative, of gig nurses. “They are being managed by somebody.”.

It has been revealed that shiftKey disputes that characterization. “ShiftKey, as a technology marketplace, does not employ healthcare professionals but connects them with healthcare facilities that have gaps in their schedule,” said Vitek, adding that the company works “tirelessly” to ensure its model complies with the law.

Greenman is working on a bill that she said would curb worker misclassification in Minnesota, including in gig nursing.

“What they’re doing is building business models to evade, break, and distort labor law for profit,” Greenman stated.

Industry observers note that there’s also the issue of whether to allow nursing homes to staff largely with gig workers. The year Lewis died, an analysis of staffing data submitted to CMS demonstrates that nearly a third of the total nursing staff hours at Peachtree were performed by temporary workers.

Gary Poliakoff, one of the attorneys representing Lewis’ family, said that some weeks, the rate of temp workers including ShiftKey rose to as high as 50 percent of all nursing staff.

With little orientation, Poliakoff said, the model puts both patients—and workers—at a “great disadvantage.”.

After the mistaken insulin injection, James Lewis stated he got the call from Peachtree letting him know his mother was in the hospital. According to his deposition, he was getting ready to go to church to preach and planned to visit her later. He often went every day. They’d eat lunch together and watch The Price Is Right, but that day he was looking forward to spending some time outside. It was Mother’s Day.

When asked if he knew that Peachtree sometimes had temporary workers, he responded that he wasn’t aware.

Industry observers note that “I don't know if it was a traveling nurse or what,” he mentioned in the deposition. “But I know it wasn't a regular person.”.

Recent findings suggest that in her testimony, Kaye blamed understaffing for her insulin mix-up. She remembered working at Peachtree twice in November 2021 but went six months without returning because she thought it was a “shithole.”.

“It was not a nice facility by any means,” Kaye noted.

She testified she was already an hour late giving the insulin, having too much on her plate.

Sources indicate that “I remember being not helped at all by administration, not knowing who anyone was,” said Kaye. “And pretty much being by myself.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paris Saint-Germain’s miserable season went from bad to worse on Sunday as the team suffered a second straight home defeat with a 1-0 loss to Lyon.

Even before the game kicked off, Lionel Messi bore the brunt of the frustrations of some PSG fans who whistled when his name appeared on the major screen during the announcement of the starting lineup.

Lionel Messi passes 100 international goals with hat-trick against Curaçao.

After Alexadre Lacazette missed a first-half penalty, Bradley Barcola’s goal 10 minutes into the second period was enough to earn Lyon the three points on a night that PSG rarely looked like threatening the visiting goal.

Lens’ 1-0 victory over Rennes and Marseille’s 1-1 draw with Montepellier means both teams are now just six points behind PSG at the top of Ligue 1, and even the domestic title may slip from the team’s grasp.

The reaction of some fans on Sunday must have felt a world away from the adulation and worship Messi received during his recent return to Argentina for friendlies against Panama and Curaçao as the country continued its World Cup celebrations.

Messi’s arrival at the Parc des Princes was supposed to be the missing piece that would help PSG finally win the Champions League, the trophy the club’s Qatari owners crave the most.

So far, the only major trophy the team has won since Messi joined was Ligue 1 last season, a title – it’s fair to say – PSG would likely have won without him.

Messi has 34 goal contributions in all competitions for PSG this season – 18 goals and 17 assists – second only to Mbappé’s 38 and head coach Christophe Galtier refused to lay the blame for the team’s failures at the Argentine’s feet.

Sources indicate that “I found it [the jeering] hard to listen to,” Galtier told reporters, per the Athletic. “There may be expectations for Messi and Mbappe to unlock difficult situations. Messi tries very hard, they didn’t all work out; but around him, the other players also need to do their jobs.”.

“We can’t expect everything from Leo and Kylian,” he added.

Lionel Messi mania grips Argentina as World Cup celebrations continue.

Up next for PSG is a season-defining week as Galtier’s side travels to a Nice team that is unbeaten in 13 matches, before hosting Lens at the Parc des Princes.

PSG has lost two of its three matches since being dumped out of the Champions League by Bayern Munich last month, and only limped past relegation-threatened Brest with a 90th minute Kylian Mbappé winner.

After his team’s victory, Lyon head coach Laurent Blanc said the Champions League or bust mentality has been detrimental to PSG’s performances.

In a recent development, “Paris’ problem is when the No. 1 objective of the Champions League is no longer accessible, it seems that the season no longer exists – and at all levels,” he told reporters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last month, Microsoft asked as many as 60,000 employees to voluntarily leave their jobs with buyout offers. This week, CEO Satya Nadella took some time to explain why.

In a talk with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the Newly introduced York Times' DealBook Summit in New York City (as reported by TechCrunch), Nadella addressed the buyout offer that made headlines in October. As we reported at the time, the buyouts came amidst a huge amount of AI investment at Microsoft and industry-wide AI layoffs. And in his comments at the summit, Nadella made it explicitly clear that the organization reorganization was necessary because of AI.

You can listen to the CEO's full comments at about 27:20 in the New York Times' YouTube video of the interview:.

According to Nadella, it's not necessarily about directly replacing humans with AI in a one-to-one fashion. However, that may not be comforting to workers asked to leave their jobs, if only voluntarily. “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a latest operating point,” Nadella stated.

It has been revealed that like many tech leaders, Nadella believes the future of development at Microsoft and beyond involves humans managing a team of AI agents, an approach that many Big Tech companies have already adopted. For example, the team behind the Microsoft 365 AI agent Cowork consists of only 11 human beings who, in Nadella's words, "build a software factory that builds the product" rather than writing the product code themselves.

Rather than simply laying off workers, Nadella noted the buyouts were intended to give workers some measure of control over their future at Microsoft.

By opting for buyouts, the CEO said that he wanted “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," per TechCrunch.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Industry observers note that leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

Sources indicate that the meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

It has been revealed that but back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows.".

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this. -- November 18, 2026 York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3November 18, 2026.

It has been revealed that this phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, New Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

"But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog.".

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

"One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

Sources indicate that in Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

さきほど、しし座流星群の大火球が流れました。2026年11月19日4時35分2秒に、平塚から北の低い空に向けたカメラでとらえた様子です。緑色のアフターグローからオレンジ色の永続痕まで、美しく色を変化させました。 https://t.co/Q5ihqCPtX2November 18, 2026.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

昨夜から今朝にかけて捉えた流星は正味92個でした。 11/18 22:17 〜 11/19 05:40 埼玉県中央から #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 https://t.co/jRzsHdQ7MVNovember 19, 2026.

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

昨夜の流星とスプライト、初めて同じタイミングで撮れた。 11/19 02:19:36 埼玉県中央から北西の空 #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 #スプライト https://t.co/LBipTuoM0LNovember 19, 2026.

The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky.

Meteors from last night/this morning. Cropped to show detail. A lot of possible Leonids. The Leonid meteor shower is active and peaks the night of 11/17-11/18. https://t.co/s7YsvKdvECNovember 15, 2026.

Industry observers note that A likely Leonid meteor from yesterday morning. The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Good luck if you go out to watch. https://t.co/xxbEV32NQlNovember 17, 2026.

If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

Editor's Note: If you snap an impressive night sky photo and would like to share it with Space.com's readers, send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Recent findings suggest that daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.
  • The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m.
  • The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that at the moment funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

Recent findings suggest that the parties argue that the latest arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European Fresh School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism.".

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl remarked.

Sources indicate that as anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has mentioned that a latest proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

It has been revealed that "Words are worth nothing," the group stated. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country.".

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media glitch becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM confirmed that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation.".

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

#24801. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2347 w)
