📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ferguson was sent off in just his fourth game as Glentoran manager.

It was a night of unfortunate firsts for Duncan Ferguson at Solitude on Friday.

The Everton great suffered his first defeat as Glentoran boss as they were edged out 3-2 by Cliftonville in an Irish Premiership thriller.

He also received his first red card as a manager, after picking up nine during his playing career, in the first half for protesting the decision to award Cliftonville's first goal after he perceived a foul in the build-up.

The defeat ended Glentoran's eight-game unbeaten run in the league and leaves them well off the pace in pursuit of their first league title since 2009.

While he has delivered with his animated touchline antics, Ferguson has so far struggled to get much out of his side on the pitch.

Ferguson sent off as Reds beat Glens in thriller - report and highlights.

Highlights: Cliftonville v Glentoran.

The Glens were second best for much of the first half in north Belfast, with Cliftonville dominating possession and creating the better chances.

Still, the awarding of the Reds' first goal was controversial as it looked like defender Jarlath O'Rourke had been pushed by Liam McStravick, who then teed up Joe Sheridan to score the opener on 38 minutes.

Ferguson was incensed that the goal stood, protesting while his side went up the other end and scored an equaliser through Cal Weatherup's deflected strike a minute later.

Such was the vehemence of his words towards the officials, referee Ben McMaster brandished a straight red card and Ferguson was forced to make the long walk to the tunnel all while being jeered by Cliftonville supporters.

"I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul. It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader, I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a significant set of boots to fill," noted Ferguson's assistant Gary Bollan.

His side looked to have received a stern talking to from Bollan at half-time as they were much more competitive after the break.

They responded to Brian Healy putting the Reds ahead once again with a fine James Douglas strike on 86 minutes, which looked to be enough to secure a point and continue their unbeaten run.

However, they failed to stop midfielder Sheridan, who waltzed into the box before firing into the top corner two minutes later to seal a win.

Glentoran's fifth league defeat of the campaign leaves them 14 points behind pacesetters Linfield.

Former Crusaders captain Colin Coates, who was on co-commentary duties for the game for BBC Sport NI, believes Ferguson and the club have "a lot of work to do" to get back challenging for major honours.

"Look at the squad, there is work to do in January and next summer," he added.

It has been revealed that "Duncan Ferguson will use this next few months to assess what he has, what he wants to keep and what he needs to bring in to make them competitive. Every time I watch them I want more from them.

It has been revealed that "There is a real lack of quality particularly at the top end they don't look like they can hurt teams aside from Jordan Stewart. A lot of work and soul searching to do and players will be playing for their futures.".

Stewart was suspended for the game at Solitude and was a substantial miss while Ferguson will hope to get more out of Conor McMenamin and the fit-again Pat Hoban, who both came on in the second half.

The Glens face two games against Larne, one in the BetMcLean Cup on Tuesday and one in the league next Friday and Ferguson will hope to mastermind two big results to really kick-start his reign.

Sheridan scored two fine goals in Cliftonville's victory.

For Cliftonville, it was a case of another major performance under the lights on a Friday in front of a raucous Solitude crowd.

The Reds beat Larne 4-2 at the same venue a fortnight ago and key in their two big wins in recent weeks has been teenage midfielder Sheridan, who is growing in stature for Jim Magilton.

The 19-year-old broke into the senior squad last season after a fruitful six-month spell at Queen's University in the 2024-25 campaign.

He won the club's Young Player of the Year award last season and was a rotation option, but he has kicked on again this year and firmly established himself in a midfield three with captain Rory Hale and Dean McMaster.

The next step for the talented Northern Ireland under-21 international is adding goals and assists to his game and he certainly delivered on Friday.

Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman said he showed "composure" for both his goals, first to curl home from close range, then to weave his way into the box and place the ball in the top corner.

In a recent development, "It was a really good performance from him. He's becoming a mainstay in the team," Leeman added.

The victory moves Cliftonville to within a point of the Glens and with games against struggling Ballymena United and Bangor to come, they will hope to embark upon another winning run to continue their surge up the table.

#24734. 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, upcoming forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife.
  • In a recent development, the evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago.
  • It has been revealed that now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, upcoming forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

In a recent development, the evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

It has been revealed that now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling upcoming support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

In a recent development, "I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," mentioned Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?".

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings.

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Recent findings suggest that surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," stated Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans.".

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.".

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths.

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

Sources indicate that the results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls revealed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing important fresh evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

In a recent development, A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

The researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

It has been revealed that additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal Upcoming Clues to Egypt's Dark Past.

Recent findings suggest that the findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve vital clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

Sources indicate that "If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" remarked Campbell. "Still, this study shows how much latest information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one.".

Chelsea have been fined Â£150,000 by the Football Association as part of a punishment for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants during an FA Cup third-round win at Charlton Athletic in January.

The club have also been warned about their future conduct and had an action strategy imposed on them in relation to the offence.

"Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief," mentioned an FA statement., external.

Chelsea admitted the charge but had an appeal against the fine issued by an independent regulatory commission rejected.

The FA's written reasons stated that although the discriminatory chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

"We unequivocally condemn this behaviour," said a Chelsea statement., external "Sectarian abuse - chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group - and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary.".

The FA itself was fined by Uefa for a similar incident of chanting, from England's away support during their Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a massive agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump stated after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

Recent findings suggest that he remarked that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," stated Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," remarked Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

According to recent reports, "Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Industry observers note that "Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," mentioned Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he remarked.

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having stated late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners.".

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar prepares for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he stated.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:.

Recent findings suggest that "Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Recent findings suggest that daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, noted Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts mentioned there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," noted Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya mentioned.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

In a recent development, "And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now.".

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

To Kim Kardashian, it isn’t rocket science to be skeptical of this historic event.

According to recent reports, the Kardashians star revealed to scientist Dr. Kate Biberdorf that she is still in the camp of not believing the 1969 moon landing happened.

“I’m a, like, we-didn’t-land-on-the-moon kind of gal,” Kim told Biberdorf during the Nov. 19 episode of The Kardashians, while Scott Disick added, “Not a chance we landed on the moon.”.

Similarly to NASA’s fiery reaction when Kim first shared her theory last year, Biberdorf wasn’t giving any space to the Kardashian family’s claims.

It has been revealed that “I definitely think we landed on the moon,” the Notre Dame science professor argued. “We’ve done it six times.”.

However, the family didn’t seem convinced. In a separate talking head, Khloe Kardashian expressed that she’s indulging her sister’s conspiracy despite the expert opinion proclaiming otherwise.

Industry observers note that “Did we land on the moon? No,” Khloé said. “Does she think we did? Yeah.”.

Kim first raised eyebrows for her moon landing theory during a 2025 episode of The Kardashians, when she shared her opinion with All’s Fair costar Sarah Paulson.

In the clip, Kim argued that Buzz Aldrin—who was the second person to walk on the moon after Neil Armstrong—claimed the moon landing wasn’t scary, which she saw as proof it was all a mirage.

In a recent development, “There was no scary moment,” Kim told Sarah, “because it didn’t happen. It could’ve been scary but it wasn’t because it didn’t happen. So, he’s gotten old and he’s slurring everything.”.

As the SKIMS founder put it, “So I think it didn’t happen.”.

For her part, Sarah wasn’t entirely convinced, but admitted, “I’m gonna go on a serious deep dive.”.

#24727. Tech Report: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

Tech Report: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to latest research led by Stanford Medicine.
  • According to recent reports, the study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful new way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline.
  • In a recent development, to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to latest research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers.".

According to recent reports, the study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful new way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

In a recent development, to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss.

It has been revealed that the latest scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," noted Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.".

Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang stated. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be.".

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

Industry observers note that zhang recognized that this approach could overlook notable biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he said. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.".

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

The Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

Industry observers note that they examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

Sources indicate that the comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas revealed greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance.

Industry observers note that the team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores showed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, key differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

In a recent development, people whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao remarked. "Our model indicates comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.".

A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging.

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements indicated some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he said.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

It has been revealed that despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Industry observers note that zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially shows a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

For example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he said. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.".

Sources indicate that although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important upcoming direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; Latest York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

‘Incredibly frustrating’: prestigious fellowship applications close in just 21 hours

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.
  • Swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship.
  • Industry observers note that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.

Swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship. On 14 November, he stayed up through the night completing the form and coordinating with referees across different time zones.

Industry observers note that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking. When he returned to submit it at around 8.50 p.m., applications had closed. The fellowship had reached its limit of 800 applications within 21 hours of opening.

Chowbey is not alone. Many researchers around the world found themselves unable to submit applications last Sunday and took to social media to vent their annoyance.

“It is incredibly frustrating to invest so much time and effort into developing a strong scientific project, only to discover that the timing of the application process may put some researchers at a disadvantage — especially when you open the system on Sunday and close it the same day,” wrote Ida Skubis, an AI researcher at Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland, on the social-media platform LinkedIn.

The Humboldt Research Fellowships support researchers from abroad to conduct research in Germany, providing €3,000 (US$3,300) a month for postdoctoral researchers and €3,600 a month for experienced researchers. Fellowships can last for 6–24 months for postdocs and 6–18 months for experienced researchers.

The fellowships and awards are recognized internationally, which is why they are so competitive, says Marcela Hernández, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a former fellow. “Being a Humboldtian is a mark of academic distinction. It has an exceptional international network.”.

A spokesperson for the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in Bonn, Germany, said in a statement to Nature that it had not anticipated that the application cap would be reached within 24 hours of opening. The foundation introduced the cap this year because it has seen a large increase in applications since 2024. It holds application rounds in March, July and November.

The spokesperson said that as more researchers have used AI to help prepare their applications more quickly, the volume of applications has increased. Humboldt does not prohibit the use of generative AI in applications, nor are applicants required to declare AI use.

Industry observers note that simon Hammann, a chemist at the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart, Germany, supported a research proposal as a prospectiveacademic host for someone who was able to submit their application successfully. He notes that opening the call on a Sunday disadvantaged researchers with family and caring responsibilities. “That should definitely be changed.”.

The Humboldt spokesperson said that the foundation advertises the date when applications will open, but that unfortunately the date fell on a Sunday this time.

It has been revealed that “We recognize the impact this had on those who were unable to apply, particularly given the challenges of coordinating availability over a weekend. We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” the spokesperson stated.

They added: “We will take this as an opportunity to continue reflecting on and improving our processes” to “find a transparent and fair solution”.

In a recent development, these days, you'll be hard-pressed to find a laptop for under $1,000 that doesn't have any major compromises. That's even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It's a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It's not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, no, but then again, it's hundreds of dollars cheaper.

In a recent development, it might be well over two years old, but I still find myself recommending the Surface Laptop from 2024. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You're limited to only the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it's the best price I've seen on this laptop this year so far. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

According to recent reports, there is a newer version, which comes with the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I've found that it's still quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you're OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you're sold on the more premium design of the Surface Laptop, this is the one to get.

According to recent reports, with the MacBook Neo selling for $649, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $750, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn't seems like a great position to be in for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is on sale often, this is $100 cheaper than I've seen it over the past few weeks.

Sources indicate that the HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it's not on sale right now). It's only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer.
  • Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.
  • After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer.

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

Sources indicate that "I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward.".

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?".

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL.

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds.

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007.

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported Â£316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

It has been revealed that "It's a massive challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis.".

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills notes it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

According to recent reports, "If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established.".

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need.".

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed.

#24722. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (936 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
  • Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s?
  • In a recent development, "Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

In a recent development, "Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today.".

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?".

Recent findings suggest that his straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

In a recent development, by 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

Recent findings suggest that to cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

According to recent reports, there are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

In a recent development, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They at the moment own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

It has been revealed that over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

Recent findings suggest that if the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

According to recent reports, he suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices.".

This article was originally published in German.

Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, legacy retailer Gap Inc.
  • It has been revealed that it was a newly created role as the organization tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform.
  • "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.

It has been revealed that it was a newly created role as the organization tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye.

"Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it.".

She stated it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.

"Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson remarked at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation.".

Recent findings suggest that in another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the company, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap.

"I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," mentioned Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form.".

Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman noted, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing.

"Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.

But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts mentioned audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original.

The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.

As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.

It has been revealed that "The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience.".

At the same time, he remarked, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.

The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.

"The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael said. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly.".

Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, stated Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

"I think it's a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you're seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies," he mentioned. "I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content.".

That's where retailers might tap creators, Akaks remarked, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.

"I do think there's a world where we're going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they're owning together," he stated.

Once those companies get consumers into the store, they're also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick's Sporting Goods offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.

According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach and Ralph Lauren saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers' average basket size.

"The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it's experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow," said Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.

Yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract latest ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn't necessarily a given.

In a recent development, "The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics," AlixPartners' Eshelman remarked. "The fundamentals are still there, and if you're going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can't mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour.".

Industry observers note that anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

In a recent development, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain noted on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”.

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

According to recent reports, instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

In a recent development, yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” indicates Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”.

According to recent reports, “It is all about the spicing and the texture,” indicates the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”.

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists.

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

Recent findings suggest that from such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

According to recent reports, bourdain, a native Upcoming Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:.

But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed/.

The trembling earth resounds his tread/.

Clap in his ample fist a blade/.

And legs and arms and heads will cut/.

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his organization Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

According to recent reports, for Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

Best Mexican food: 23 dishes to try.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie mentioned.

Sources indicate that “From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”.

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he claims. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”.
