I Play Rocky review: Can this crowd-pleaser be an Oscar contender?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that rocky is such a truly iconic film that it's easy to forget its very existence is a miracle.
  • Peter Gamble's screenplay begins with the future Hollywood star going by Mike Stallone (Anthony Ippolito), hitting auditions with his brawny shoulders and distinctive accent, and getting cast as thug #2 if he's lucky.
  • Enter Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb), a smart and dedicated young woman who pushes Mike not only to write the roles he wants to play but to make a mark with his real name, Sylvester Stallone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rocky is such a truly iconic film that it's easy to forget its very existence is a miracle. I Play Rocky is the story of how that miracle was built by the blood, sweat, and tears of an unknown actor and aspiring screenwriter named Sylvester Stallone.

Peter Gamble's screenplay begins with the future Hollywood star going by Mike Stallone (Anthony Ippolito), hitting auditions with his brawny shoulders and distinctive accent, and getting cast as thug #2 if he's lucky. At this point, he's living on the streets, finding comfort in a stray puppy he's taken in, and doing some light sex work to keep them both fed. But all he needs to start the path to Rocky is one person to believe in him.

Enter Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb), a smart and dedicated young woman who pushes Mike not only to write the roles he wants to play but to make a mark with his real name, Sylvester Stallone. Together, they move from the cold streets of Latest York to the sunny hills of Los Angeles. He writes out script after script by hand, then she types them up so he can hopefully sell them. When Rocky finally catches the attention of respected producers, it might seem like a happy ending. But there's one catch that Sly lays down: "I play Rocky.".

Industry observers note that stallone, as an unknown, fought tooth and nail to be the center of the movie he dreamed up to make him a star. But at every step, a upcoming challenge presented itself. His underdog story reflects Rocky's — sometimes literally recreating scenes from the Oscar–winning sensation. But as successfully entertaining and heart-warming as I Play Rocky is, will it be able to stand out to the Academy in this year of extraordinary cinema?

Industry observers note that well, for starters, director Peter Farrelly previously won over the Academy with Green Book, which scored Best Supporting Actor for Mahershala Ali, Best Original Screenplay (for Farrelly and his co-writers), and Best Picture. That too was a feel-good film inspired by true events. And to its credit, I Play Rocky is less likely to earn the backlash that Green Book did, as it doesn't engage in problematic racial stereotypes.

Recent findings suggest that what I Play Rocky does offer is a cast that absolutely crackles onscreen. Ippolito takes on a difficult role as Stallone, because even a casual movie fan can recognize this A-lister's signature cadence and tone. To his credit, Ippolito is terrific in the role. Not only does his take on Stallone feel familiar, but he also avoids the trap of making it feel like an impression. This becomes clearer when he's tasked with re-enacting classic Rocky scenes, where the physicality of Stallone demands to be even more in sync with the man himself.

Sources indicate that beyond getting the feel of Stallone right, Ippolito has an easy charisma that sparks chemistry with every scene partner, be it his onscreen lover Robb, a pair of bickering producers (P. J. Byrne, Toby Kebbell), his dynamic Rocky co-star Carl Weathers (Stephan James), or his lumbering dog, Butkus. Ippolito's Sly is radiant with life and determination, a screen presence that Stallone brought to Rocky.

It has been revealed that and around him, he's bolstered by terrific supporting players. Byrne and Kebbell prove a terrific comedy duo, turning exposition about movie deals into entertainment. Robb shines, despite being in a role that is an achingly cliched Supportive Wife with no complexity. (As presented here, Sasha has no desires beyond what makes Sly happy.) James is electric, an unapologetic scene-stealer who becomes Sly's ally. Tracy Letts is solidly sneering as an antagonistic studio exec, and Jay Duplass is brightly funny as self-proclaimed asshole director John G. Avildsen.

According to recent reports, together, they craft a fish-out-of-water showbiz comedy slash underdog drama that is undeniably rousing and wonderful. So, why won't that be enough for I Play Rocky to be a contender?

In a recent development, on the ground at the Toronto International Film Festival, when I Play Rocky made its World Premiere, the buzz was thunderous and immediate. Following its first screening, the press lined up in a massive theater for the press-and-marketing-screening to see for themselves if this movie could live up to the hype. For those who've never been, that's a tough crowd, almost daring filmmakers to impress them. And adding to the difficulty, this screening was at 8:30 AM on a Sunday, when most sane people would prefer to be in bed. I was in that audience, and frankly dubious I'd enjoy Farrelly's latest, as I tend to think his best film is Dumb & Dumber. (I remarked what I said.) To my surprise and delight, I roared with laughter and cheers, as did the hundreds around me. Speculation sparked that this movie would win the festival's audience award, hands down. And the People's Choice Award out of TIFF can often be a bellwether for Oscar success. According to Awards Radar, since 2000, 33 People's Choice winners have gone on to become Best Picture nominees at the Academy Awards, with nine of them winning — including Green Book. But despite the buzz, I Play Rocky didn't win this honor.

It has been revealed that the People's Choice Award went to La Bola Negra, a Spanish drama by directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi that explores queer identity over 85 years in Spain. That film, while extraordinary, is not a crowd-pleaser. It's 159 minutes long, interweaves multiple narratives, and is inspired by four pages of a play written by poet Federico García Lorca before he was assassinated by a fascist government. It's tragic, romantic, and cerebral. And it has all that in common with the International People's Choice winner, Elsinore, which focuses on Scottish actor Ian Charleson's performance of Hamlet as he was dying of AIDS.

Industry observers note that where I Play Rocky had brilliant buzz on its debut, it was a runner-up at the end of the festival. And as award season heats up, there's a trend emerging, favoring tragedies over feel-good stories. Another example: TIFF opened with the inspiring docudrama Being Heumann, helmed by Sian Heder, director of the Best Picture winner CODA. While this follow-up has been praised for its representation of people with disabilities in telling the story of disability advocate Judith Heumann, the praise for the movie itself has been muted.

Meanwhile, Calvo and Ambrossi are gathering buzz for the Best Director honor, and Andrew Scott seems a frontrunner for his heart-wrenching performance in Elsinore. And then of course, there's the significant wooden horse in the room: The Odyssey.

According to recent reports, being both an unadulterated hit with critics and a box office smash that not only brought audiences back to theaters, but also sold out IMAX theaters across the country, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is going to be hard to beat this Oscar season. He brought together a sprawling cast, shot on location, and used practical effects to extraordinary ends to reimagine Homer's Greek epic for a modern, mainstream audience. It is a collision of poetry, craftsmanship, and performance that is absolutely astounding. The Odyssey highlighted succinctly why movies still matter, connecting a story that's centuries old to contemporary politics without feeling like it was talking down to its audience.

It has been revealed that there, I Play Rocky falls short. While it is a movie about the importance of cinema, which the Academy loves, it's a look back that feels more a celebration of Stallone than it does a story urgent to now. And in the final act, Farrelly gets carried away in recreating Rocky, pulling in one scene after another to diminishing returns. While his film is still a sensational experience, its final act leans too heavily into the audience's presumed love of Rocky, instead of trusting in their interest of the story being told. And hey, in another year, that might not have been a fatal flaw; it might not even be one that will keep I Play Rocky from some big nominations. But even though I'd argue I Play Rocky is a better movie than Green Book, I wouldn't bet Farrelly's film has a fighting chance against its TIFF peers, much less Nolan's epic.

I Play Rocky was reviewed out of the Toronto International Film Festival. It opens in limited release in the U.S. and UK on Nov. 6, before going nationwide in the U.S. on Nov. 20. #24700. Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1373 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.
  • It has been revealed that it’s not just old; it’s also really far away.
  • Recent findings suggest that the expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.

It has been revealed that it’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

Recent findings suggest that the expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

In a recent development, but if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit quickly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Recent findings suggest that enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

Sources indicate that but what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo says in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

According to recent reports, and it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

Sources indicate that as Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He mentioned that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

Voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.).

Industry observers note that for Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally launched to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really major gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

Newton’s second law of motion states that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

It has been revealed that let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

Industry observers note that not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

Sources indicate that it’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) with director of football Jason Wilcox.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

According to recent reports, in a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

According to recent reports, "Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he noted. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

In a recent development, "We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that.".

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds Â£1bn.

Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears Â£100m.

Andrey Santos has started four Premier League games for Manchester United since his Â£50m summer move from Chelsea.

It has been revealed that wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Sources indicate that carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for Â£116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for Â£85m.

It has been revealed that instead, United paid a combined Â£118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' Â£35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

Recent findings suggest that "We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending Â£40m, Â£50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team.".

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

In a recent development, "I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he mentioned. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad.".

Pochettino on his arrival at Man Utd.

Berrada noted there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the challenges are.

He stated he was wary of reading too much into data that highlights United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now.".

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very notable player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me.".

Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean.
  • Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food.
  • A newly introduced study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more crucial when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A newly introduced study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

It has been revealed that "We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," remarked first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish.".

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth.

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

Recent findings suggest that as animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

It has been revealed that however, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source.

Industry observers note that to investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

Sources indicate that A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu.

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different.".

Sources indicate that modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea.

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Recent findings suggest that its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

Sources indicate that the difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean.

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

In a recent development, the available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Recent findings suggest that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, noted the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private organization.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the firm last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people mentioned.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

According to recent reports, foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The organization has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak stated in an April television interview.

According to recent reports, that April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

According to recent reports, eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump mentioned in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands.".

Sources indicate that eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

According to recent reports, "Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight.".

In a recent development, eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts.".

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the firm, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

In a recent development, instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, remarked a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

Industry observers note that insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Recent findings suggest that pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, remarked the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

Recent findings suggest that that setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people remarked. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the firm's financial disclosures, the people said.

"This is what happens in a company with no governance," noted one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?".

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The tech giant was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle firm Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.

Sources indicate that while some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, mentioned as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

According to recent reports, federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump mentioned. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, declared his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

It has been revealed that brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in Upcoming York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

It has been revealed that using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

Recent findings suggest that “You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

Recent findings suggest that by the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

In a recent development, T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Tech Report: Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you?
  • Sources indicate that based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
  • Recent findings suggest that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Sources indicate that based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

Recent findings suggest that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

Recent findings suggest that this being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

Viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

Recent findings suggest that after sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a new variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

Sources indicate that that vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

According to recent reports, drusilla is one of the latest characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a big chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace quickly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Industry observers note that sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating upcoming version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

Recent findings suggest that no spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

Recent findings suggest that but while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

According to recent reports, throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up states "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

It has been revealed that anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.).

It has been revealed that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine.

Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.

Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk stated he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also stated Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.

In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".

Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk.

It has been revealed that "In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.

According to recent reports, "Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong.".

Mudryk also noted the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld vital information and documents" from his lawyers.

BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

It has been revealed that presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that the 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

In a recent development, second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin.".

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she mentioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That indicates what's at stake," she mentioned.

In a recent development, the prize winner also remarked she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

Sources indicate that in his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim remarked journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he mentioned, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

Recent findings suggest that "I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he stated.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he stated.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

In a recent development, so far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue.".

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from.".

Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set upcoming records as the earliest ever observed.
  • According to recent reports, quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos.
  • Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set upcoming records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

According to recent reports, quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

According to recent reports, launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

It has been revealed that "These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," indicates Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics.".

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars.

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

Sources indicate that "Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting.".

According to recent reports, among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn.

Industry observers note that two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

Sources indicate that these discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

Recent findings suggest that "The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level.".

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies.

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Recent findings suggest that their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where upcoming stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an notable glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

According to recent reports, these quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," claims ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants.

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground.".

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

In a recent development, although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide fresh clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Significant Bang.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.
  • The tech giant notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov.
  • You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

The tech giant notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms.

You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower.

"The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat debuts and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above.

It has been revealed that starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger.

Recent findings suggest that as SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The manufacturer plans to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight.

SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight, Starship's 15th to date, which rolled out on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico.

In a recent development, that wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights. Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does.

SpaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the tech giant managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try.

According to recent reports, and Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the tech giant has sent to low Earth orbit. The first set was deployed on Flight 14, which introduced on Sept. 28.

#24687. Tech Report: Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1301 w)
