Tech Report: Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard.
  • In a recent development, by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release.
  • So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard. If you're not playing it but are reading this, we can guess why.

In a recent development, by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release. If that's the case, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of the year — and possibly all time. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

Industry observers note that the primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

By all accounts, GTA 6 is a pretty fantastic video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

One thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

Lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Industry observers note that both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing. If you're not sure whether to buy a PS5 or the Xbox Series X/S, keep scrolling for a breakdown of the pros and cons.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

Both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is at the moment out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

Recent findings suggest that there are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that you won't like the game, though so far, most people who have played it have come away with positive impressions. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the fresh game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

Maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There was a lot of anxiety on the internet prior to the game's launch surrounding the potential differences between the different console versions. The good news is that the game is out and has been fully tested by experts, and the verdict is that you almost can't go wrong with GTA 6 on any platform.

Digital Foundry is an outlet and YouTube channel that offers expert-level tech analysis of games, and they have a fairly comprehensive guide to the different console versions of GTA 6. According to DF, both the PS5 and Series X versions run at the same resolution and target the same frame rate, with some performance dips on both in more intense sequences. In other words, the base PS5 and Series X versions are roughly the same, though the PS5's controller does have exclusive haptic feedback features for gameplay like driving cars.

There is also the matter of the PS5 Pro and Xbox Series S consoles, though. DF claims the PS5 Pro is the best version of the game, with a sharper resolution and higher-quality shadows to go along with smoother performance. That was to be expected. Sadly, it sounds like the Series S version is probably the least desirable build of the game. Its visuals have been marginally downgraded with a lower resolution and some reduced visual settings, but more importantly, DF's analysis found that the frame rate can dip below 20fps in extreme circumstances.

Industry observers note that we do have good news for Xbox Series S gamers, however. Mashable Editorial Director Eric Miller has played the game on Series S and has had a positive first impression so far. If you have no other way to play GTA 6, it should work, but it will be reduced in quality compared to the others.

There is technically a way to play GTA 6 without buying a latest PS5 or Xbox, but it's not a viable alternative for most people.

Industry observers note that to be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

If game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not said anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

#24683. Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
📖 Baca

Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it was 5:55 a.m.
  • Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget.
  • It has been revealed that reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

It has been revealed that reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

It has been revealed that but here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

In a recent development, if the latest debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

In a recent development, this development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that for 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding upcoming investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

In a recent development, what's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

According to recent reports, russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary.".

In a recent development, the rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are looks for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, people born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

Industry observers note that the pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

According to recent reports, anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This also means that interest rates on newly introduced loans are not set as high. This is an notable point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

It has been revealed that the prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year.".

Tom Brady is a seven-time Super Bowl champion.

American football great Tom Brady is looking to invest in Chelsea through ownership group Clearlake Capital.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner has recently divested his stake in Championship club Birmingham City, which he bought into following Tom Wagner's Knighthead Capital takeover in 2023.

It now appears he could move into Chelsea, where he has a positive relationship with influential co-owner Behdad Eghbali, having been a star guest at the after-party following the club's Club World Cup triumph in 2025.

Brady would have no voting rights or control at Chelsea, although the ownership group could look to appoint him to the board if it suited all parties.

The move is not remarked to be linked to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter's Â£950m sale of their stakes to Clearlake Capital, which must be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss remains a significant minority stakeholder at Stamford Bridge.

The investment is also not part of a funding round, according to senior sources, and is not intended to dilute Clearlake Capital's control.

Latest Update: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an crucial role in physical and mental well-being.
  • In a recent development, the discovery could be especially vital for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an crucial role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

In a recent development, the discovery could be especially vital for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

According to recent reports, to investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

In a recent development, "Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy noted. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

In a recent development, one possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

In a recent development, when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy noted.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

Recent findings suggest that even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Sources indicate that someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

According to recent reports, "As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy remarked. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

In a recent development, the research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Recent findings suggest that because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

Materials provided by University of Missouri-Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#24677. A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1829 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Sources indicate that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Sources indicate that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

Recent findings suggest that the research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

Sources indicate that in 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising key questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this key protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," claims first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Recent findings suggest that proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she notes.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

Sources indicate that in laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

In a recent development, MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

Recent findings suggest that "These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Industry observers note that mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

According to recent reports, the findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Industry observers note that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

Industry observers note that "Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

According to recent reports, arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie notes. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

Sources indicate that the possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It has been revealed that scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says.

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC indicates the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

It has been revealed that further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz remarked in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

Sources indicate that the implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

In a recent development, dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the latest research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

It has been revealed that A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did.
  • Industry observers note that to err is human, science endeavours included.
  • Industry observers note that sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan.

Industry observers note that to err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Industry observers note that sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” claims Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”.

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

Sources indicate that for the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

According to recent reports, in the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise highlighted a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

According to recent reports, I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them rapidly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is crucial; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn important lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo.

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

It has been revealed that back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

According to recent reports, then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

It has been revealed that so I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

She kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Sources indicate that metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a latest professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

Recent findings suggest that I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

Industry observers note that I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a new species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley.

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

Sources indicate that I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a substantial deal for our laboratory in 20164.

According to recent reports, in 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a big genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

In my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

It has been revealed that two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

Industry observers note that when I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s big phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the fresh species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Sources indicate that before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more latest things.

Now I realize how crucial it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

It has been revealed that palaeontologist Catherine Badgley claims that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay.

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

It has been revealed that in the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, showed me a fresh way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

In a recent development, in well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a big gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

In a recent development, but the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

#24671. Industry News: How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1356 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
  • Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.
  • In a recent development, "I've always been a bit cautious about this matter in recent years," he stated, as reported by the news outlet RND.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

In a recent development, "I've always been a bit cautious about this matter in recent years," he stated, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he unveiled a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently.".

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also mentioned AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail manufacturer, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market.".

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It demonstrates that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

It has been revealed that "But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play.".

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they noted AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he rolled out a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, but Herrmann remarked it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

Industry observers note that "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she remarked. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens.".

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

It has been revealed that however, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living.".

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," stated Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible.".

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

Industry observers note that AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?".

Industry observers note that this, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?".

#24670. On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid

On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid.
  • Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system.
  • Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth.

Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway.

Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010. Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

The primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth.

It was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) debuted the probe on May 9, 2003, with plans for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005.

That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines.

Still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005.

Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has noted.

During its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report. Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft.

Industry observers note that "The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time. There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway.

"After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had remarked. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005.

In November 2010, five months after Hayabusa's sample-return capsule touched down in Australia, JAXA unveiled some good news: Hayabusa did collect 1,500 dust grains from asteroid Itokawa, samples that were jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite is collector mechanism not firing.

The ultimate success of Hayabusa spurred the creation of another sample-return mission by Japan: Hayabusa2.

That probe launched in December 2014 and arrived at asteroid Ryugu (REE-ooh-goo) in 2018. It collected its own samples and returned them to Earth in December 2020. The Hayabusa2 probe is now on an extended mission to the asteroid 2015 BM510, which it will fly by in April 2028. It had planned to land on a strange asteroid 1998 KY26, but suffered engine trouble that made that rendezvous impossible.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA releases MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from Newly introduced York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She right now lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

Rivian, Lucid, Scout CEOs aren’t counting on Democrats to restore EV federal support after midterm wins

💡 Key Takeaways
  • electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.
  • That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.
  • "We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

"We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

Legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe remarked it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that.

Sources indicate that "We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe said Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done.".

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

"You know, they say, 'Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it.".

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

CNBC previously reported that House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, remarked she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

"I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, mentioned. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for.".

Scout's Keogh stated if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

Industry observers note that "I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh stated. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer.".

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

"Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, stated Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive.".
