Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • According to recent reports, although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

According to recent reports, although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how vital the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

In a recent development, the discovery shows that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

Dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

It has been revealed that for roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

In a recent development, however, the most important finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

Industry observers note that this suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

Industry observers note that polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

Recent findings suggest that one example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

Sources indicate that the problem is that these habitats cannot swiftly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, upcoming ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

The discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An crucial question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

Researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is right now participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

The findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

#24653. Latest Update: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Latest Update: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.
  • Recent findings suggest that known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk.
  • Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Recent findings suggest that known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, demonstrated DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

It has been revealed that the "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Recent findings suggest that parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

Recent findings suggest that "When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

In a recent development, women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

According to recent reports, in 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska remarked she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Sources indicate that dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, stated the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated.".

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she noted.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," mentioned Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan.".

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

It has been revealed that earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

According to recent reports, "I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she remarked.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, noted they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she stated.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk noted abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

According to recent reports, one reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents stated they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • Sources indicate that the stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer fresh clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

Sources indicate that the stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

According to recent reports, until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

It has been revealed that the newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

In a recent development, despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

The latest discovery provides an notable breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

Recent findings suggest that "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," remarked lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," stated Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

After the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Sources indicate that both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

It has been revealed that dr. McSweeney stated, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her firm handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.
  • According to recent reports, “I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Golloria can’t conceal her thoughts on Huda Beauty’s apology.

After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her firm handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.

According to recent reports, “I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov. 20 Instagram post. “Speaking from both my experience as a shade consultant and as a dark skinned woman whose shade options are directly affected by this decision, I don’t think Coco Truffle should replace Coffee Cake. And that’s just the honest truth.”.

The TikToker explained that she heard Huda Beauty’s reasoning that Coffee Cake wasn’t doing well with consumers, but added that she didn’t think the two shades were “interchangeable,” noting that “a shade occupying a similar depth in a range doesn’t necessarily mean it serves the same complexions.”.

Sources indicate that “You’ve stated several times that you want to better serve dark skinned women, and part of that is listening to the women telling you that Coffee Cake already works for them,” the 25-year-old continued. “That feedback should help guide what you preserve as you expand the range.”.

She also added that darker skinned women “deserve variety in both depth and undertone,” and that having both shades would help create that inclusion. Instead, Golloria shared in her own Instagram caption that she felt Huda Beauty was “doing what's easiest for the brand instead of what's needed by the women you say you want to serve.”.

“Inclusion means making room for our differences,” she wrote, “not asking us to settle for whatever is most convenient for you to offer.”.

As for Kattan, while the beauty founder did not reply to Golloria’s comment, she explained in her apology video that she was sorry for how the conversation about the shade replacement had been handled with Golloria, especially as it was happening during a busy time for the brand and when Kattan herself had to undergo emergency surgery for a ruptured breast implant in April.

According to the 43-year-old, her team found that Coffee Cake was “not something that a lot of people have shared positive feedback with us on,” adding that they “definitely thought we could make it a lot better.”.

Industry observers note that the decision led them to launching Coco Truffle as a replacement for Coffee Cake, first as a pressed powder, then as a loose powder—although it was not yet widely available.. But after hearing from their consumers, Kattan realized they should have done a better job being more inclusive with their shades.

“Inclusivity is not about, ‘Yes, done, check, we're inclusive.’ That to me is some of the things that are wrong with the industry,” she noted. “It's 2026. We can do better. We can do better and I think brands should be doing better in 2026.”.

And while they will be reworking Coco Truffle to make sure it’s available “as rapidly as possible,” she also regretted fully removing Coffee Cake from their lineup.

“We should have kept it in stores,” Kattan stated, “because at the end of the day, if some people liked it, we should have kept it in stores until there was something better available.”.

She also once again apologized for not having better communicated all of this to Golloria initially, although she was hopeful that the beauty influencer and Huda Beauty fans would appreciate Coco Truffle.

“I'm hoping to give you guys a shade that you guys really, really love, and all the beautiful rich skin tone girls and boys feel really represents them,” Kattan shared, “and is perfect for their skin tone.”.

Massive-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this holiday season, major-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs.
  • "We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," remarked Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.
  • Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this holiday season, major-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," remarked Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year.".

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Recent findings suggest that most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania stated.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives noted.

According to recent reports, UPS CEO Carol Tomé remarked on the firm's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers.".

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for substantial-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Organization's annual forecast. Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

"The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers remarked. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf.".

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding upcoming team members.

Industry observers note that "Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania remarked.

Industry experts noted they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry.".

Amit Regev, CEO of drone tech giant Flytrex, remarked the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev noted.

According to recent reports, retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September mentioned it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex at the moment delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev said. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones.".

#24648. German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, is Germany's economy back on the up?
  • At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen.
  • The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I stated here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

In a recent development, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz stated in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

In a recent development, given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz noted when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

It has been revealed that the chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

In a recent development, but these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that "We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she mentioned.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Sources indicate that germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that however, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," mentioned Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

Sources indicate that the so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, remarked the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz stated there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

It has been revealed that according to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

Sources indicate that if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

According to recent reports, but innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

Upcoming evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

In a recent development, the intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a upcoming study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The executive list for Billboard Canada Women in Music has dropped.

The list spotlights changemaking women from across the music industry — from radio to streaming, labels, performance rights organizations, publishing, live production and more.

Each honouree shares their proudest achievements, hard-earned lessons and advice to young women getting into the ever-shifting industry today.

The list is led by Executive of the Year, Live National Canada chief commercial officer Melissa Bubb-Clarke, who has helped execute one of the biggest ever years for the live music company, including the second season of the latest Rogers Stadium in Toronto, the opening of the Drake-partnered History Ottawa and the reopened RBC Amphitheatre.

Kristy Fletcher wins the Impact Award for her work as president of music education charity MusiCounts and chief operating officer of CARAS, the organization behind the Juno Awards.

The list also spotlights this year’s award winners, a star-studded list of global and Canadian stars.

The top spot is hip-hop star Cardi B, who is recognized as Global Woman of the Year and will accept the honour on Nov. 24 at Rebel in Toronto. She will be joined by fellow award winners Bebe Rexha, Summer Walker, Chxrry, Blond:Ish, Faouzia, Tia Wood and more.

Find the full list here and the full Billboard Canada Women in Music programming lineup here.

It’s a substantial week of honours at Billboard Canada as the 2026 40 Under 40 list has also dropped.

From independent label heads and managers building robust domestic infrastructure to scale talent globally, to live promoters championing community, the honourees are helping Canadian artists thrive at home and on the global stage.

Each honouree was asked what is exciting and challenging for the next generation of music executives, and their responses inform what you will read here. Many echo the same sentiments: Canada has the talent and ambition to break out on the global stage, both the next generation of artists and executives. To get them there, we will need to foster resources and mentorship at home first. Judging by this year’s 40 Under 40 honourees, we are well on our way.

The list is headed by 40 Under 40 Visionary Award winner Kaytranada, who has quietly become one of Canada’s biggest global success stories.

From making beats in his bedroom to climbing the ranks of Montreal’s nightlife scene, he’s made history in the dance world with his forward-thinking, signature blend of R&B, funk and hip-hop. He is the first electronic/hip-hop act to take home the Polaris Music Prize in 2016 and the first Black and gay producer to ever win a best dance/electronic album Grammy Award, in 2021. He’s toured festivals around the world, as well as arenas and even stadiums as a featured act on select dates of The Weeknd’s record-breaking After Hours Til Dawn Tour.

“Coming from Saint-Hubert [Quebec] and Montreal, then crossing over internationally, it’s not just anything,” he claims in an interview with Billboard Canada. “I celebrate everything and I’m happy with still being a force in electronic music. I never take it for granted.”.

Find the full list of honourees here.

Your mid-twenties are a period of major transformation — just ask Gracie Abrams.

“There’s this kind of lust and regret, and you see your own patterns as you evolve and enter upcoming relationships or friendships,” the chart-topping singer-songwriter tells Billboard Canada from a New York hotel.

Those ideas are central to the artist’s second No. 1 album on the Billboard Canadian Albums chart, Daughter from Hell. Today (Nov. 20), she expands the universe with five deluxe tracks, deepening the album’s exploration of change and growth during the transformative decade.

Extending the album’s lifecycle and building onto that world, she explains, has always cosmically aligned with her going on tour.

“That feels like the final form of the album to me, when we’re in community around it,” she says.

It has been revealed that A memory that Abrams vividly remembers is when The Secret of Us and “That’s So True” went No. 1 back-to-back on the Nov. 23, 2024 and Nov. 30, 2024-dated Billboard Canada charts when she was an opening act on the final leg of Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.

“I have such core memories about my Canadian audience because we’ve had some nuts milestones while we’ve been in Canada,” she says. “When [The Secret of Us] went No. 1, we got to be on stage and I got to say thank you to that many Canadian people [at sold-out Rogers Centre in Toronto]. I was so grateful that I could directly say it.”.

In a recent development, she continues: “I just find it insane that people outside of your own village know who you are. It feels very lucky. The generosity and energy that we’ve been shown by our Canadian audience has blown my mind.”.

Abrams pinpoints her two appearances at Montreal’s Osheaga, calling them “a core memory.” The sets bookmarked two different times in her career. She first performed in 2022 during the day on one of the main stages, and later was slotted for an evening set in 2025 on the same stage, but drew a much larger near-headline crowd.

#24645. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1680 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • According to recent reports, researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • Sources indicate that the findings raise crucial questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But fresh research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

According to recent reports, researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

Sources indicate that the findings raise crucial questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," states Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

According to recent reports, deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an notable role in carrying away waste products.

According to recent reports, that earlier discovery led to a new question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

It has been revealed that previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially crucial.

It has been revealed that to investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

Industry observers note that the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

In a recent development, the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings showed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

It has been revealed that the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

Industry observers note that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

To measure this response, the researchers demonstrated volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group demonstrated a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Recent findings suggest that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes says. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have important implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

None of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants indicated signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

Recent findings suggest that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

While older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

Industry observers note that "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Massive Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo.
  • However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Newly introduced Major Five” for wildlife photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Sources indicate that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Massive Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Newly introduced Major Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The Newly introduced Substantial 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green notes that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he notes.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

Recent findings suggest that in total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, notes Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” claims Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Substantial 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

According to recent reports, as well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “Upcoming Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she remarked.

“The Newly introduced Massive 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

Now this is a revelation to wig out over.

According to recent reports, sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr.’s paths didn’t officially cross until the late ‘90s on I Know What You Did Last Summer, but as they recently learned they had more in common than they realized. According to recent reports, “We always joke that the closest connection I had to my husband's side of the family,” Gellar told E! News in an exclusive interview, “was that for a small time I went to the same high school that my husband's dad went to, and that was like sort of our one thing.”.

After all, though Gellar—mom to Charlotte, 17, and Rocky, 14, with Prinze—is a native New Yorker, her husband was born in Los Angeles and grew up in New Mexico. (His dad Freddie Prinze, however, hailed from New York.).

Sources indicate that she continued, “Then through Ancestry, we found out that our grandparents lived less than two miles away from each other in the Bronx at one point, which they could have potentially known each other. That's kind of crazy.”.

Recent findings suggest that for the Buffy the Vampire Slayer star, who teamed up with Ancestry for its Gathering the Good initiative, it was an opportunity to explore her own family’s legacy while also looking at the spirit of giving through history. So, tracing how her loved ones made the journey to America in the 1890s at the same time philanthropist Lena Sittig space was creating what is now considered to be the modern toy drive, really hit home how interconnected the mission is.

“I learned that my grandmother was coming over on a ship at 16 years old, right when Lena was having her idea for this,” she shared. “It’s kind of crazy how the world intertwines, and it just reminds you that you're just such a small part of such a bigger picture.”.

It’s especially poignant as diving back into her roots has not always been a focal point for Gellar.

“It's funny, I didn't really spend that much time thinking about my history and my ancestry because I try so hard to live in the moment,” she explained. “And when Ancestry came to me and talked about what they wanted to do, I thought, ‘What a great idea to be able to learn acts of kindness, acts of goodness that your family may have been a part of that you never knew.’”.

As the Cruel Intentions alum knows, ‘tis the season to pay it forward. “The holiday season gets so dramatic—presents and all that,” she noted. “And I always look for what are the things that you could give someone that are really meaningful.”.

So, the 49-year-old posited, “What's more meaningful than learning about where you came from and your family and things you may not have known?”.

To Gellar, it all comes back to Lena Sittig and her Brooklyn Christmas Tree Society, and how her idea is sparking change so many generations later. In fact, the Ringer actress teamed up with Ancestry to fulfill Christmas lists for Children’s Aid.

Sources indicate that “So often, I think we think, ‘Well, I'm one person. What can I do?’ And then you see something like that, and you realize, oh wow, one person can do a lot,” she told E!. “But then to take it that step further, and maybe there's people in her family had no idea they were related to her.”.

“Can you imagine going back in your history and finding out that one person in your family was responsible for millions of children's gifts all over the world because they had this idea?” Gellar added. “I think it's really special.”.

And it’s an experience Gellar wants to send far and wide, teasing what many of her loved ones—not to mention anyone looking to explore the impact their family has made on others—may be getting under the tree this year.

According to recent reports, “There's something for me about the how tangible it was,” she admitted. “I saw signatures, I saw writing. it makes it seem just much more real to you than just getting an email that claims, ‘You know you came from here’ like, seeing their actual signatures at Ellis Island. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has begun its journey home to Earth.

According to recent reports, the robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) today at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

If all goes according to strategy, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at about 4:55 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). There will be no livestream for its reentry and splashdown. (Today's departure webcast did not feature live footage of the moment of undocking, as it occurred during a gap in coverage of the high-bandwidth signal needed for video.).

In a recent development, the Dragon released Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it's the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

According to recent reports, the capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It will bring a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

It has been revealed that "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an revision on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

In a recent development, dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

Recent findings suggest that editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking.

AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • In a recent development, "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

In a recent development, "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Industry observers note that jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is at the moment teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

According to recent reports, even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she stated.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a fresh topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

According to recent reports, not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, remarked class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

Industry observers note that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

Sources indicate that that's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In a recent development, in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she remarked.

Sources indicate that there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, stated: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

In a recent development, müller stated one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

Everything about BepiColombo entering Mercury orbit on Saturday
