💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.
  • Sources indicate that the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other.
  • A major engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robotic spacecraft that has spent eight years looping around the inner solar system is finally set to lock into orbit around Mercury, the planet closest to the sun.

Sources indicate that the European-Japanese mission, called BepiColombo, carries two science probes stacked on top of each other. One is the European Space Agency's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO. The other is Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, nicknamed Mio.

A major engine burn should steer the pair into a regular, closed orbit that passes over the planet's north and south poles on Saturday, Nov. 21.

Sources indicate that mercury is the least explored planet in the inner solar system. Only two spacecraft have ever visited it, NASA's Mariner 10 in the 1970s and Messenger in the 2010s. That will make BepiColombo just the second mission to orbit Mercury and the first to put two orbiters there at once. One probe will observe the planet itself and the other will study its space environment. Scientists hope the results will show how rocky planets like Earth form and change when they're born close to their star.

Recent findings suggest that reaching Mercury is actually harder than getting to Pluto. Falling toward the sun isn't the only problem. It's bleeding off enough energy to avoid overshooting the planet.

Industry observers note that bepiColombo rolled out on Oct. 20, 2018, on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. For most of the trip, it rode on a separate engine module that used ion thrusters. These engines push the spacecraft by firing charged particles out the back. The force was about as strong as the weight of two sheets of paper resting on your hand. But the thrusters ran for two years, carrying the spacecraft about 6 billion miles.

The spacecraft also used gravity from nearby planets to bend its path. It swung past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times. In Sep. 2024, it passed within about 100 miles of Mercury, the closest any spacecraft has ever flown past a planet. The trip wasn't smooth sailing. The engine module's solar panels started losing power, so the team had to slow down and push back the arrival date. Controllers detached the engine module on Sep. 3.

Sources indicate that "It's a very difficult mission and very challenging because we are flying into a very, very harsh environment," Bruno Sousa, ESA's head of operations definition and engineering, said during a livestream that day. Mercury's surface can drop below -290 degrees Fahrenheit at night and climb above 750 degrees during the day. The spacecraft gets baked from two sides — by sunlight and heat rising off the planet.

Recent findings suggest that the arrival itself is unusual. Most missions hit the brakes hard and drop straight into orbit. BepiColombo is coming in slowly instead, and it gets there in steps. First, it drifts into Mercury's gravitational grip on a loose, irregular path that doesn't loop all the way around the planet. Engineers call this "weak capture." Spacecraft operations manager Ignacio "Nacho" Clérigo said no one has tried it with a planet before, only with moons. Saturday's big burn swaps that wandering path for a true orbit. It starts out as a long, lopsided oval, and the spacecraft fires its engines about every three days to reel it in.

As the orbit tightens, a series of handoffs follow. On Dec. 9 and 10, the European orbiter releases Mio into its final orbit. Full science work should begin in April 2027.

Mercury holds plenty of puzzles. It's unusually heavy for its size. Apart from Earth, it's the only rocky planet with a magnetic field surrounding the whole planet. Scientists want to learn whether Mercury's huge liquid core has a solid center. Others blueprint to measure magnesium, potassium, and calcium in the space around Mercury. Those elements offer indirect clues about what the surface is made of.

Sources indicate that the mission is named for Italian mathematician and engineer Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo. His work on using planets' gravity to steer spacecraft helped make the earlier Mercury missions possible as well as BepiColombo's long, looping route.

Tech Report: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • It has been revealed that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

It has been revealed that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A new study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

Industry observers note that planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

On Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

Earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

In a recent development, uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

Recent findings suggest that "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," mentioned Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

Industry observers note that ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

It has been revealed that their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

According to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

Sources indicate that "Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," mentioned Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

It has been revealed that these dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

Researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

Auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an key stepping stone," remarked Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

According to recent reports, the ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

Industry observers note that the research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the new dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

Industry observers note that even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require new spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nguyen Quynh Anh's reign as Miss Universe Vietnam has officially come to an end.

The beauty queen was initially suspended in October when private messages speaking negatively about other pageant participants became public, and now the organizers have revoked her title due to Nguyen's conduct while under suspension.

Recent findings suggest that the concerns occurred while Nguyen was barred from performing in all "artistic performance activities" related to Miss Universe for six months, the show’s organizers, Five6 Entertainment, announced in a Nov. 18 statement, according to Tuoi Tre News.

In addition to being suspended from events for the group text—which included runner-up Trinh My Anh—containing derogatory remarks about past winners, fellow contestants and judges, the model was ordered to pay a fine, the outlet said.

However, when the influencer attended a community event while banned from representing the pageant, the production company, per Tuoi Tre News, remarked her appearance caused issues that "affected the image of Miss Universe Vietnam and its organizers.".

In addition to promoting her title while suspended, the organizers stated that the 27-year-old delayed signing her management contract in order to prioritize a "mental health condition" amid the transitional period. Still, the team noted they learned Nguyen signed an exclusive contract with a competitor management agency and "continued accepting performance engagements and attending events without reaching an agreement with Five6.".

According to recent reports, in response to the initial backlash, the competition's runner-up, Trinh, apologized on Instagram. Meanwhile, Nguyen released an Oct. 13 statement transcribed by the outlet where she apologized "to the women concerned and everyone affected by this incident, especially the audience.".

Recent findings suggest that "I understand that holding a beauty queen title does not make me incapable of making mistakes," her statement continued. "However, the title requires me to be more mindful and careful about my words, conduct and responsibilities, even in seemingly minor matters.".

It has been revealed that E! News has reached out to Nguyen Quynh Anh regarding the recent conduct allegations but has not yet heard back.

The release noted that her title was formally revoked after reviewing the conditions of holding the crown, the outlet stated.

And given the unexpected exit, Vietnam will not send a competitor to the global Miss Universe finale on Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.
